text:
*Interview with Madame Odile Monnier, in the dining room. Second interview of the night.*

MATTHEY: Madame, thank you for coming down. I know the hour and I know the night. Tell me about the evening in order, as you remember it.

MME MONNIER: We dined at the usual time. When the temple bell struck nine, my husband made everyone show their watches. He does it every year.

MATTHEY: And what did the watches show?

MME MONNIER: Félix's watch showed twenty minutes to nine. Aurèle scolded him for it. He tells each of us what is wrong with our watches. He is never satisfied with a watch that is not his own.

MATTHEY: Was there any other disagreement at table?

MME MONNIER: Monsieur Girard wanted to buy the rights to the repeater. He and my husband quarrelled about the price. They were not quiet about it. I did not think it would be the last time.

MATTHEY: What happened after dinner?

MME MONNIER: The doctor and I played piquet in the salon. We played without a break. The temple struck ten while we were at the cards.

MATTHEY: Did you continue playing?

MME MONNIER: We played on until he went out to fetch his cigars.

MATTHEY: Did you look at the clock when he went?

MME MONNIER: No. I did not look at the clock when he went. I was counting my cards, Inspector, not the hours.

MATTHEY: Did he say anything as he left?

MME MONNIER: He asked me to play for him. I sat down at the piano at once. I played Chopin until he came back, and I stopped when he came in.

MATTHEY: Do you recall the time when he returned?

MME MONNIER: A moment after he came back, the hall clock struck eleven. That is the only hour I can give you with any confidence.

MATTHEY: Thank you. Let us speak of the household. How long have you been married?

MME MONNIER: A long time. I was a pastor's daughter from Neuchâtel. I knew what I was marrying, a man who loved his work more than most things. I shall not pretend otherwise for your notebook.

MATTHEY: And Doctor Vauthier?

MME MONNIER: Casimir has been our friend since we were young. He attended Jules, Aurèle's brother, in his last illness. He is the oldest friend this house has. I would not have a word said against him in my presence.

MATTHEY: I did not intend one.

MME MONNIER: No, but you have the look of a man who is writing things down.

MATTHEY: Tell me about Félix.

MME MONNIER: Félix owes money. Some of it, I believe, is owed to Monsieur Girard. My husband knew it and would not lend him a centime. Félix made jokes about it at dinner, which is what he does when he is frightened.

MATTHEY: Did your husband have enemies, Madame?

MME MONNIER: I cannot tell you what a man like my husband had. He had watches, and opinions about them. The second was the more dangerous.

MATTHEY: Is there anything you wish to add?

MME MONNIER: Only that you will forgive me if I do not weep in front of you, Inspector. I have done my weeping over Aurèle's temper, and I have no tears left for his death.
